title: DHS Ends Duration of Status for F-1 and J-1 Visas, Imposes Four-Year Cap
excerpt: The Department of Homeland Security has finalized a rule replacing the decades-old flexible visa system with fixed admission periods capped at four years, effective September 15. Universities and immigration experts are urging international students abroad to return to the U.S. before the deadline.
body:
• The DHS final rule, published July 17, eliminates “duration of status” for F-1, J-1, and I visa holders and caps initial stays at four years, taking effect September 15, 2026.
  • Students needing additional time must apply to USCIS for extensions, with requests subject to background checks, biometric screening, and fraud reviews — a shift from the current university-managed system.
  • The post-graduation grace period for F-1 students is cut from 60 days to 30 days, and restrictions on changing majors, transferring schools, and pursuing additional degrees are tightened.
  • India, which sends the largest number of international students to the U.S. — roughly 330,000 in 2023-24 — faces an outsized impact, with New Delhi saying it is “actively monitoring” the situation.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security published a final rule on July 17 that dismantles the nearly five-decade-old “duration of status” framework governing how long international students and exchange visitors can remain in the country. The regulation, which takes effect on September 15, replaces the flexible system with fixed admission periods capped at four years for holders of F-1 student visas, J-1 exchange visitor visas, and I visas for foreign journalists.

Universities across the country are now advising international students currently abroad to re-enter the United States before September 15, since those who arrive after the effective date will be admitted under the new, more restrictive framework. Students already in the U.S. will automatically transition to the new system, with their remaining authorized stay capped at four years from the rule’s effective date, according to DHS.

What changes under the new rule

Under the previous policy, established in 1978, F-1 students could remain in the U.S. for as long as they maintained enrollment in their academic program without a fixed end date. J-1 exchange visitors received similar treatment starting in 1985. The new regulation replaces this with an exact admission date based on initial program length, not to exceed four years.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Ci-H5kjUq5A

Students who need more time to complete their degrees — and more than half of first-time bachelor’s degree recipients take longer than four years — must now apply directly to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for an extension. Those applications will be subject to background checks, biometric screening, and fraud reviews. Doctoral students, who spend a median of nearly six years on their dissertations, face particular uncertainty.

The rule also shortens the post-graduation grace period for F-1 students from 60 days to 30 days and imposes tight restrictions on changing majors, transferring between schools, and pursuing additional degrees at the same or lower level. Foreign journalists on I visas will be limited to 240-day stays, with Chinese journalists capped at 90 days.

Universities and experts push back

“At a time when global competition for talent is intensifying, this policy sends exactly the wrong message,” Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, said in a statement. “It tells the world’s brightest students and scholars that the United States is becoming less welcoming, less predictable, and less committed.”

https://x.com/helen44767171/status/2079140541657411607

The proposed rule drew more than 20,000 public comments, with the overwhelming majority opposing the change. Sixteen state attorneys general, major higher education associations, and scientific societies filed detailed objections. The University of Virginia, among many institutions, has told students that the effective date “may be subject to change pending congressional review and likely litigation.”

A Brookings Institution analysis published on July 20 estimated the regulation could cost the U.S. economy $72 billion to $145 billion annually over ten years — more than 22 times the $3.3 billion in cumulative costs that DHS itself projected. The analysis, drawing on a National Academies-commissioned report, found that roughly half of surveyed international Ph.D. students and postdoctoral fellows said they would not have come to the U.S. if they had known duration of status would be eliminated.

“For nearly half a century, the outdated ‘duration of status’ system has compromised national security and created an environment ripe for immigration fraud.”

— Markwayne Mullin, DHS Secretary

Impact on Indian students

India sends the largest number of international students to the United States, with approximately 330,000 enrolled in the 2023-24 academic year, according to India’s Ministry of External Affairs. The new rule is expected to disproportionately affect Indian nationals, many of whom pursue STEM graduate degrees that regularly exceed four years.

New Delhi has signaled concern. Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India is “in contact with the American government” and will “take up those issues with the US side so as to minimise the difficulties that our people face.” He noted that visa and immigration policies are “sovereign functions of any state” while emphasizing India’s commitment to supporting its diaspora.

The regulation adds to an already difficult landscape for Indian students navigating expanded travel bans, stricter social media vetting at consulates, and reduced visa validity periods introduced in recent months.

What happens next

The September 15 effective date is not guaranteed. The rule is subject to congressional review under the Congressional Review Act, and four bipartisan congressional representatives have already urged DHS to delay implementation. Legal challenges are widely expected, following a precedent from 2018 when a similar DHS attempt to end duration of status was blocked by a preliminary injunction.

For now, immigration advisors at universities including UVA, USC, and Boston University are telling students to ensure their travel documents — including valid passports, unexpired visa stamps, current I-20 or DS-2019 forms with recent travel signatures, and financial documentation — are in order for re-entry. NAFSA continues to update its guidance as the September 15 deadline approaches, and institutions are planning town halls and FAQ sessions for affected students.

International students contributed $42.9 billion to the U.S. economy and supported more than 355,000 American jobs in the 2024-25 academic year, according to NAFSA. Whether the rule survives legal and congressional scrutiny may determine whether those contributions continue.
